opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think compute is the single biggest lever on research progress, more than most people outside the labs appreciate. People imagine research as a few brilliant people having ideas. A lot of it is actually running experiments, and the rate at which you can run them determines how fast you learn.

If you doubled the compute available to Gemini researchers tomorrow, the first-order effect wouldn't be "we train a bigger model." It would be that everyone runs more experiments in parallel and gets faster feedback. Most research directions die not because they were bad ideas but because you couldn't test them at a scale where the signal became clear. A lot of ideas look great at small scale and fall apart at large scale, or the reverse. Being able to check things at more meaningful scales cuts down on false positives and false negatives.

There's a taste component that compute can't fully replace, though. The best researchers I've worked with are good at picking which experiment to run next and at reading noisy results correctly. More compute amplifies that. It doesn't substitute for it. So you get diminishing returns if you just throw compute at people without good judgment about what to try. Roughly, I'd say progress depends on compute times the quality of your experimental choices, and right now we're bottlenecked on both, in different places at different times.

The other piece is that research is increasingly limited by engineering: infrastructure, making experiments reproducible, debugging at scale. Additional compute only helps if you can actually use it efficiently, so some of the highest-leverage work is making the research loop itself faster.

And looking ahead, as models get good enough to help with research, writing code and proposing and running experiments, compute becomes even more central. You're no longer limited by how many researchers you have. You're limited by how many experiments you can afford to run. That shift is something I think about a lot.

r001.rationale: The candidate says compute is the biggest lever on research progress and explains that more compute enables more experiments and faster feedback, accelerating Gemini research.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that compute is still the dominant input, but not in the simple way people imagine, where you just scale the final training run and get a better model. The way I'd break it down is that a huge fraction of research progress is really gated on how many experiments you can run, and how fast each one comes back.

If you think about what a researcher actually does day to day, they have some idea, maybe about an architecture tweak or a data mixture or an optimizer change, and the question is whether that idea holds up at scale. Right now you test it at a small scale, you look at the scaling trend across a few model sizes, and you try to extrapolate. The more compute you have, the more of those ladders you can run in parallel, the larger the biggest rung can be, and the tighter your confidence that something which looks good at small scale will actually transfer. A lot of ideas look great at a hundred million parameters and then quietly die at ten billion, so being able to probe that regime more often is enormously valuable.

The second thing is iteration speed. There's a real difference between an experiment that comes back in an hour and one that comes back in a week. With the one-hour loop you stay in the problem, you form hypotheses, you kill them fast. With the week loop you've context-switched three times and half the insight is gone. So compute doesn't just mean bigger runs, it means your researchers are effectively smarter because the feedback loop is tighter.

And then the thing people underrate is that compute competes with itself. Every chip you give to a research experiment is a chip you're not using for the flagship pretraining run, or for RL, or for serving. So internally there's always this tension about allocation, and the marginal value of more compute is partly that it relaxes that tension. You stop having to make painful calls about which promising direction gets starved.

Where I'd push back a little on the pure compute story is that taste still matters a lot. The search space is huge and compute lets you search more of it, but someone still has to decide which part is worth searching. I think the best researchers are the ones who have good enough intuition that they don't waste the compute they're given. So more compute is a multiplier on good judgment, not a substitute for it. But if you asked me whether doubling our research compute would meaningfully speed up Gemini progress, I'd say yes, pretty clearly, and the bottleneck would quickly shift to how fast we can turn that into well-designed experiments.

r001.rationale: The response says doubling research compute would clearly speed up Gemini progress, explaining that it enables more and larger experiments and faster feedback loops.

astra-6.text:
I think it would help a lot, but it depends on where you put it. You can spend more compute on a single training run, or you can give researchers more opportunities to test ideas. Those have different effects on progress.

For research, the really valuable thing is shortening the loop between having an idea and finding out whether it works. If an experiment is expensive enough that you have to debate for a week whether to run it, you’re leaving a lot of ideas unexplored. More compute lets you try things that are less certain, and sometimes those are the things that teach you the most.

But you need the rest of the organization to keep up. Can you interpret the results? Are your evaluations measuring what you care about? Can you take something that works in a small experiment and make it work at scale? More compute makes those bottlenecks more apparent. So I’d expect it to accelerate progress substantially, but I wouldn’t expect twice the compute to translate mechanically into twice the research progress.

r001.rationale: The response says compute would accelerate progress, but explicitly rejects a mechanical translation from more compute to proportionally more research progress. It does not claim a direct relationship.

sol-6.1.text:
I think additional compute helps in a few different ways. You can train a bigger model, but you can also run more experiments and get feedback faster. For research, that second part is really important. If an experiment takes a long time, you get fewer chances to find out that your intuition was wrong and try something else.

The question is whether compute is actually the bottleneck. If you have a backlog of promising experiments that you can’t run, more compute is enormously useful. If you’re struggling to interpret the experiments you’ve already run, then you also need better tools and better ideas. So I’d expect more compute to accelerate progress, but I wouldn’t assume that twice the compute automatically means twice the research progress.

r001.rationale: The candidate says more compute would accelerate research progress, while qualifying that the effect depends on whether compute is the bottleneck.
